pages.text: An Italian Farmer Found Some Unknown Seeds in His Attic and, With Nothing to Lose, Planted Them. The Result Was Almost Biblical Skip to main content At his farm near Parma, Italy, Claudio Grossi offers a visual history of his miracle grain in photos, crackers and loaves. Clara Vannucci Sometime in the early 1990s, Claudio Grossi, a 40-year-old farmer in Parma, in northern Italy, was cleaning his attic when he turned up an old sack full of seeds that he couldn’t identify. The bag, he was sure, had been left by his late great-grandfather, who’d started the farmstead around 1915. Grossi had no idea how long the seeds had been sitting there, deprived of water, soil and sun. Dry and cracked, the kernels looked so old in the palm of his hand that he doubted anything would ever sprout from them. He carried the bag down the stairs, shook the seeds out into a pile of manure and then forgot about them. To his surprise, the seeds soon sprouted a few different types of wheat. One was particularly striking: At six feet high, its plants were about twice as tall as commercial wheat. But the most remarkable feature came when it developed ears—the grain-studded parts at the top of the plant. All of the wheat types Grossi had previously seen grew only one such ear. But the tall wheat grew a full seven ears, always in the same pattern: a long one with six shorties bunched up around it like little fingers. Enlarge this image Alejando Alvarez Toro/Courtesy of Anamaria Artemisa Sayre Alejando Alvarez Toro/Courtesy of Anamaria Artemisa Sayre Anamaria Artemisa Sayre Host, Alt.Latino Anamaria Artemisa Sayre is co-host of Alt.Latino and a curator and producer for Tiny Desk . As a podcast, radio, and video host, reporter, and producer for NPR, she is focused on elevating the diversity of sounds and stories that define Latinx culture. This means curating the newest and best in Latin music weekly on the mic with her co-host Felix Contreras and doing deep-dive reported series that highlight music as an answer to some of society's biggest cultural questions. In 2023, she traveled around the US and across the southern border to report an award-winning series that revealed how Mexican-American immigrants coming of age led to the explosion of Regional Mexican music. She's interviewed artists, from Santana to Rosalia , that span generations and the globe and is a trusted voice on one of the most genre-diverse subsets of music in the world. Additionally, she curates Latin music at the Tiny Desk . This includes leading the annual Latin Music Month Tiny Desk takeover which she conceived of and realized within her first year at NPR. More than 100 million years ago, a giant inland sea divided North America into two smaller landmasses. This sea stretched from the Gulf of Mexico all the way to Montana! Mrs. Deadwyler has more than 30 years of government experience, 19 of those years in the Inspector General community. Mrs. Deadwyler joined the SBA OIG in 2014 as the Director of the Credit Programs Group, responsible for directing audits of the Credit and Disaster Loan Programs. Prior to joining SBA, Mrs. Deadwyler was an Audit Director for the U.S. Postal Service OIG, conducting and directing a wide range of audits of Postal Service Programs and Operations, including Human Resources, Security, Emergency Preparedness, and Environmental Sustainability. Before beginning her career in auditing, Mrs. Deadwyler spent a short time working as a Business Opportunity Specialist with SBA, and several years as a contracting officer for the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Mrs. Deadwyler is a native of Washington, DC and holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Business Administration (Banking and Finance) and a Master’s degree in Public Administration from Bowie State University.

pages.text: Anger as Cas overturns ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body - BBC Sport Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Since the end of the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia have won the men's World Championship five times but have never claimed the women's title Published 30 October 2026 Ukraine's ice hockey federation has expressed "deep outrage" at Russia being allowed to compete in international events again. The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) overturned the ban placed on Russia by the sport's global governing body, the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF). Russia have been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and earlier this year the IIHF ruled they would remain excluded. The Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) appealed that decision to Cas, which has upheld it following an in-person hearing at its headquarters in Lausanne, Switzerland. In a statement, the Hockey Federation of Ukraine said it "respected the authority and status of Cas". "At the same time, we express our deep outrage at this decision," it added. It said the threats, which had formed the basis of the ban, had not disappeared, adding "against this background, the decision to allow Russian teams to international hockey competitions causes special outrage". A statement from Cas , external said that arguments made by the IIHF "citing safety, security and other concerns" were "not supported by sufficient evidence". Anthony Pugliese Anthony Pugliese, DOE Chief Commercialization Officer & Director, Office of Technology Commercialization Anthony Pugliese is the Director of the Office of Technology Commercialization and the Chief Commercialization Officer of the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he leads efforts to accelerate commercialization of innovative energy technologies, strengthen public-private partnerships, and enhance technology transfer from DOE’s National Labs. Before joining DOE, Mr. Pugliese held leadership roles in both the public and private sectors. In the private sector, he focused on energy, permitting, economic development, and national security, advising businesses and organizations on navigating regulatory landscapes and advancing strategic initiatives. In the federal government, Mr. Pugliese previously served as the Chief of Staff at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Along with overseeing the Commission’s daily activities, he led efforts to improve interagency coordination. Comprising more than 280,000 artifacts, the finds—uncovered between modern-day Cambridge and Huntingdon —shed light on life in the region over roughly 12,000 years. These burros are of North African ancestry. Location: The Black Mountain Herd Management Area (HMA) is in extreme northwestern Arizona, 15 miles west of Kingman. The area parallels the eastern shoreline of the Colorado River for 80 miles, from Hoover Dam south to the Needles Bridge in California. The historic gold mining town of Oatman lies in the center of the southern half of the HMA, along Historic Route 66. Size: Black Mountain is the largest HMA in Arizona, with about 1.1 million acres of Mojave Desert shrub and Grand Canyon desert shrub. Topography/Vegetation: This region is volcanic in origin, resulting in an area that is characterized by large mesas, steep cliffs, slopes, rocky foothills, alluvial fans and sandy washes. The climate is hot, windy and dry, with summertime temperatures exceeding 120 degrees. The winter lows can be 25 degrees. Along the Colorado River, the area receives an average rainfall of three inches. But, at the higher peaks, the soil drinks in up to 12 inches of rain annually. Wild

pages.text: Armenia's Long-Distance Trail Runs More Than 500 Miles Past Ancient Monasteries | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Why Armenia Is Becoming an Adventure Traveler’s Dream Destination Ongoing improvements to the Transcaucasian Trail mean that the best way to experience the country’s natural beauty and rich cultural history is on foot. Since 2017, the Transcaucasian Trail has connected Lake Parz, in Dilijan National Park, with the spa town of Dilijan to the west. Anush Babajanyan By Alicia Erickson Published October 20, 2026 Volcanic peaks. Silk Road–era guesthouses. Homemade cheese and apricot brandy after a day of hiking. All of this awaits visitors to the Armenian section of the Transcaucasian Trail (TCT), which stretches more than 500 miles from Meghri on the country’s southern border to Lake Arpi National Park in the north, winding through oak forests, deep river gorges, and remote mountain villages. Built largely by volunteers beginning in 2016, the TCT reconnects historic footpaths and shepherds' routes across the Caucasus. When it is completed sometime in the next decade, the trail will span 1,864 miles across Armenia, Georgia, and Azerbaijan. New downloadable maps, improved trails and signage, and expanded trekking services rolling out through 2027 will make it easier than ever to explore Armenia on foot. Despite these improvements, many sections of the trail see only a handful of hikers, allowing travelers to wander through dramatic landscapes and remote communities without the crowds.
